utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. I note Mr. Robinson is absent today. I was advised that there's something for you, Mr. Tieger, to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. If we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think we are now in open session. Unless there are other matters to raise, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope we can conclude your evidence today. Mr. Karadzic, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everybody, and good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you -- or, rather, ask you: For 10 months in 1992, you were with UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that right, and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia is more accurate, the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then, on the 13th of December, 1992, become an adviser to the conference or in the Conference on the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, although the date is questionable. But approximately then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you remain in that post until the 12th of March, 1993? Rather, the 12th of December, 1993, I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that that was a very important advisory role in the team of Secretary Vance and Mr. Stoltenberg?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were rather more important people, I'd say. But, yes, it was a significant role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody more important -- a more important adviser on military issues than you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the force commander, and there were three of them in the time that I was there. They were formally the military adviser to Mr. Vance and Mr. Stoltenberg, but on a daily basis, certainly, I provided that intimate support. But the important issues, the force commander was always consulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a little patience, please, because I'd like to ask you whether the following posts were ones that you occupied, and I'll read it in English: [In English] "A. Three times daily situation reports on UNPROFOR operational activities." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many occasions. Sometimes it was only once a day. It depended upon the level of operational activity in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you: [In English] "B. Provide regular, usually biweekly intelligence assessments on future developments. "C. Obtain urgent information on specific operational activities as they affected ongoing negotiations." [Interpretation] Are B and C correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "D. Draft the military aspects of negotiating documents"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you: "E. Refer to the force commander major issues requiring his personal attention and agreement."

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "F. Pass information between the co-chairman and the force commander on an as-required basis."

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Pass information on ICFY activities to UNPROFOR, usually to the head of Civil Affairs"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Finally: "Attend negotiating sessions, accompany the co-chairman during his travels, and provide advice on the military practicality of various initiatives." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]: [In English] "Brigadier Wilson was intimated involved in the drafting and negotiation of the BH military agreement. It was the one document of the various peace packages formally accepted and signed by all the parties. He was also less successfully engaged in detailing negotiations over the conflict in Croatia for many months." [Interpretation] Is that paragraph correct as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Well then I'm not quite clear why in a paragraph of your statement you say you were a minor player. Is this not, after all, an important function?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, Mr. Karadzic. I simply say there were more senior and more significant people there. The ICTY had many people of ambassadorial rank assigned there, and there were significant other advisers who had the ear of the co-chairman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, did you say ICTY or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An error once again, Your Honour. ICFY, I-C-F-Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were several witnesses in court here who said that they were minor players. Now, do you have an explanation as to why the Prosecution is calling people who consider themselves to be minor players and not calling your bosses to come in and testify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not for the witness to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then the Trial Chamber will probably find an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, perhaps from the decision-making standpoint, there were people higher placed than you, but it seems to me that from the level of information, there was nobody that was above you; right? Information on military matters, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On military matters, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm a little concerned, General, and here's why: During this testimony of yours, for example, on the 21st of June, on the transcript on page 3945, you were in a quandary as to whether Nedzarici was a Serbian settlement, and then on 3944, page 3944, you weren't sure whether you -- or you said, rather, that you didn't know General Siber? Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then once again on page 3945, you did not know whether Nedzarici was under the control of the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that it was a disputed area, that the confrontation line changed over time there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I would ask Mr. Karadzic to quote the exact line back to the witness when he's taking him to transcript. When asked about General Siber, the witness answered: "I have a vague recollection of Mr. Siber, perhaps a member of the Presidency forces." So it wasn't that he didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I can't check it myself because LiveNote is not working. In the meantime, can we know when it will be fixed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quoting verbatim. I'm just asking in general terms, and that's why I'm quoting the page number. You said, on page 3948, for example, that you weren't sure whether you knew the contents of the letter from General Morillon to Izetbegovic; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which letter we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell me, General, at what distance you can see -- you can hear the outgoing fire of, let's say, a mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on how much other noise is in the area at the time. But if it is quiet, you would hear it at more than a kilometre. If there is other firing going on close by, you might hear it at 200 metres. It depends, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on page 3951, for example, you weren't sure how far the PTT building was from the center of town. How far was the PTT from the positions from which the Muslims could have shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims could have shot from right outside my window. That's a very vague question. You need to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, how far is the PTT from Marin Dvor, Bascarsija, not to mention the surrounding hills, which were also locations where the Muslims were located? So how far is the PTT building from Marin Dvor, let's say?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this level of geography that you're asking, Mr. Karadzic. I don't have a detailed knowledge. These places are meaningless to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But certainly more than one kilometre; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I restate, I don't know the geography.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 3952, you said that you didn't know the deployment of Muslim forces. Is that still your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3953, you weren't able to confirm any knowledge of the fact that we, in 1993, stopped a counter-offensive at Srebrenica and that we didn't enter Srebrenica at all. Is that still the position you maintain?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall such a counter-offensive, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was a large counter-offensive one year after the beginning of the war in Eastern Bosnia. And General, sir, we allowed armed formations in those villages to stay there. We didn't touch them for one and a half years or one year. And when we couldn't take it any more, we launched a counter-offensive. Now, do you know that there was a very large Muslim armed formation there at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, now that you've provided a little bit more information about that counter-offensive, as you describe it, I do recall that military action. I believe as a result, the enclaves in the Drina Valley were created; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is correct, thank you. Now, on page 3959, you said that you didn't know that the Serbs were expelled from the Neretva River Valley. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's still my position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it still your position that you do not know that in the Neretva River Valley, there were 44.000 Serbs living there and that the vast majority fled, most of them before the war, from the Neretva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on that same page, 3959, do you still say you don't know where the Serbian refugees came from in Nevesinje and other parts of the so-called High Herzegovina area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same page, you said that you did not know that even before the war the Serbs fled from Livno. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3960, you said that you did not know which armed incidents took place before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you maintain that position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The context of this is lost on me at the moment. I don't know in which context you're asking this, which incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know how many places were bombed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, today's Republika Srpska, how many places were bombed from Croatia before the war broke out in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the war broke out formally, Mr. Karadzic, and I'm not sure what the term "bombed" means. "Bombed" to me normally means delivered by a military aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, shelled, let's say shelled, using artillery. But let me give you an overall statement and summarise, General. Do you know that there were many shells from Croatia falling on Bosanski Brod, Samac, Dubica, falling on Novi Grad, and that this happened before the outbreak of the war, if we take it that the war broke out in Bosnia on the 6th of April, together with its recognition? So do you know how many from Croatia, and you were in charge of Croatia as well, how many combat operations there were against the Serbs in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in the period mid-January, when our military liaison officers first deployed into -- along the line of confrontation in Croatia, and mid-March or the end of March, when I moved down to Sarajevo, we were reporting the violations of the cease-fire agreement, which included firing from Croatia into Bosnia and Croatia into the Krajina, which was still part of Croatia anyway, and we were reporting incidents reported by both parties. And it was happening, often, 2- or 300 violations a day, and I'm sure some of those would have been fire from Croatia into Bosnia, and equally a lot of them were from Bosnia into Croatia. So I am aware that there was military action before the 6th of April along that northern border of Bosnia, but it was from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who could have shot at Croatia from Bosnia, General? Why are you constantly trying to strike a balance when the Serbs are victims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me to be impartial, Mr. Karadzic, and that's what I tried to be for my two years that I was associated with the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. There was a conflict with two sides participating. Both sides were firing weapons. I'm simply reporting the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, impartial does not mean to falsify the truth and falsify the events. The Serbs from Bosnia never fired on Croatia, nor did they have anything to fire at them with, whereas Croatia did many months before the outbreak of the war. So how can you say that it involved both sides? But never mind, let's move on. Now, did you know when the refugees -- the Serb refugees started fleeing from Croatia and coming to Bosnia? Do you agree that that was already the case in June and July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there in that time-frame, but I am aware that there were many refugees -- Serb refugees who had to flee Croatia, and some of them ended up in Bosnia and some went to other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 3961, you said that you did not know what happened when the Croats stormed Bosanski Brod on the 3rd of March, you don't know what happened. The Croatian Army crossed over into Bosanski Brod, and you asked me what army I was referring to. And I said that I believed they were the Croatian National Guards Corps, the Zenga, and other irregulars. What is your position now? Do you maintain your position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And on that same page, you said that you didn't know very much about the Lisbon Agreement, you weren't well informed about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On 3965, page 3965 of that same transcript on that same day, you said that Minister Doko, in June 1991 -- or, rather, that Bosnia had already had a defence minister, Jerko Doko, who became the defence minister in January 1991. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday I believe that it wasn't until late May that I became aware that there was somebody who called themselves the minister of defence, and I believe it was Mr. Doko. When he was appointed, I don't know, but I only became aware of him in late May. As you recall, Mr. Karadzic, I was not involved with any of the political parties until UNPROFOR left on the 16th/17th of May. My point of contact a couple of days after I left became the minister of defence, Mr. Doko, and he was the person I spoke to on the Presidency side until he was relieved by Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you know that Halilovic was never defence minister, he was actually commander of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're perhaps more accurate than I was in my terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 3965, you said that you did not know about the Patriotic League and its establishment or that they wanted war with the Serbs in the summer of 1991. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of the Patriotic League until you mentioned it here, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not know that up until January 1992, that is to say, two or three months before the war, the Patriotic League had its staffs and units in 103 municipalities? Actually, you've already answered this. Now, did you know that the Muslim forces -- or, rather, the Sarajevo forces had been established as the 1st Corps, consisting of the 12th, 14th, and 16th Division? You didn't know about that either. That is on page 3966.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you did not know that in Sarajevo, there were about 15 brigades with their headquarters, logistic bases, artillery, tank and mortar positions, which constituted over 300 legitimate targets. That's on the same page, 3966.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that that was the organisation of the Muslim forces within the city. I don't know that they can be described as legitimate targets unless you look at their specific deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you still maintain that the Muslim forces in Sarajevo consisted of 15.000 policemen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my estimate that there were 1500 -- around 15.000 Presidency forces there. I don't know that I've ever described them wholly as policemen. At some point in time, they became an army for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My estimate is about the size of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that brigades existed in the town of Sarajevo, with their respective numbers, the 101st and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that you reported about the 10th Mountain Brigade and that you called them extremists? I guess they were criminals. That was what one of your reports says. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 3968, you were not very clear on whether ECMM had their own people in Bijeljina and Northern Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you manage to locate the tunnel that you talked about? You said that to the south of Sarajevo, there was a tunnel, and Mrs. Plavsic also told you that the Muslims held that. Do you know of the existence of that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became aware of the existence of the tunnel. Exactly when, I can't recall. But, yes, I was aware of the existence of the tunnel. I can't recall any conversation with Mrs. Plavsic saying that. She may well have. I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On 3976, you also said that you were not aware of the ethnic picture of Sarajevo. On the same page, you also said that you did not know which areas were predominantly populated by Serbs and that were under our control. Does that -- is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with some qualification, in that I was broadly aware that some suburbs were Serb. For example, I understand Ilidza was Serb, so that would be one exception to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3980, you said that you did not know that the Muslims held Hum and that on the slopes of Hum the Muslim artillery had their positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. General, you just -- a minute ago, you said you don't remember having a conversation with Mrs. Plavsic about the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can remind you what you said yesterday. I don't have the updated page number. It's page 25, in line 15/16. You said: "I received an allegation from the Presidency representatives that there was a tunnel somewhere to the south of Sarajevo which was being used to hold a large number of non-Serb people." And then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, we're talking about two different tunnels. One is a tunnel considerably to the south of Sarajevo, where it was alleged that prisoners were held. I think the tunnel that Mr. Karadzic is referring to is the tunnel which went under the airport and was used by Presidency forces to move personnel and supplies and equipment into the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the tunnel which was located at the southern part, you had a conversation with Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the one that's alleged with the prisoners of war or detainees, yes, but not about the one under the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D1855 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your statement, General, dated the 24th of November, 1993. It's towards the end of your term as military adviser. Do you recognise the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I please have paragraph 3. It's at the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to read that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Nevertheless, I raised the issue of detention camps with both parties on a number of occasions. Each party responded that they would permit our visiting the alleged sites (whose existence they each denied), providing we first visited the other parties' camps. In one case, it was agreed that we could visit a Serb --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "-- camp alleged to exist at Pale, and a Muslim centre located in a road tunnel to the south of Sarajevo. We had to abandon the proposal when the Presidency said we could visit their location but they could not guarantee our safety. Soon after this incident, other more pressing operational tasks emerged and precluded any possibility of further investigation."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you see now that it was the Muslims that held the Serbs in a tunnel to the south of Sarajevo, not the other way around?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I believe this document rather than my recollection at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you, General, to the south of Sarajevo, towards Mostar, in the tunnel of Osenik, the Muslims held several hundred Serbs in that tunnel. And in town itself, near Ciglane, one side faces Velesici and the faces Ciglane, they held their tanks and they also held Serbs that were detained there. Do you know about that other tunnel of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you've confused me with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm putting to you: There were two tunnels. They were both in Muslim hands, and Serbs were held in both tunnels. One tunnel is in the centre of town. It's below Kosevsko Brdo, the hill of Kosevo from Velesici to Ciglane, and the other one is in the area towards Mostar, to the south of Sarajevo. And you are referring to it here. And that's when you were told that Muslims held Serbs in that tunnel. Did you know about this other tunnel in the centre of town? It wasn't hard to visit that one.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please just read the first sentence of paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I cannot specifically recall if detention campsites near Vogosca were included in the extensive lists provided to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 5: "Given the state of fighting around the city ..." Could you have a look at that sentence? It's toward the bottom of paragraph 5. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second part of paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Given the state of fighting around the city and the absence of UNPROFOR operational presence around Vogosca, I believe it would have been extremely unlikely that an UNMO could have visited that area until about September, when additional weapon concentration sites were negotiated and established in areas to the north of the city."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should note, General, for the record, it should read "UNMO operational presence."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: UNMO, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 7, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can read. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It would be a good thing if the general were to be reminded that "Newsday" reporters were aggressively asking him to confirm what it was that they had wanted. The general showed his integrity here, and he noted that as an improper thing that happened to others as well. General, is that the way it was, as I have put it, that you were asked to confirm things that were physically impossible, in terms of investigations and so on? [In English] "The UN action was outside my mandate. I further advised him that UN presence in the area was extremely unlikely during the period I was in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] What do you say to that? Do you recall this telephone call from "Newsday"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a number of conversations with this particular reporter. He had a story that he insisted upon, and a version of it that I don't believe was supported by the facts, and I simply tried to tell him the story that I knew. And he would not accept it. He was very aggressive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page, page 3: [In English] "He changed the timing of the alleged incidents from May/June to summer and late summer." [Interpretation] And then paragraph 8, to your credit, could you please read that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I am firmly of the belief that, while one cannot entirely discount a possible UN presence in the area, this article is a deliberate disinformation. This would not be the first time, nor the last occasion that the parties have attempted to discredit UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D334.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, let us have a look at 3982. You could not say when the Army of Republika Srpska came into being; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I gave an estimate of some time around about late May, when General Mladic arrived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, why did you say that the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, wore five-pointed stars on their cap? Is that not one of the stereotypes, that Serbs were inclined towards Communism?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall ever making a comment on five-pointed stars, Mr. Karadzic, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did say, though, that a group that was involved in an attack or, rather, committed an offence wore JNA uniforms and that on their helmets and caps they had five-pointed stars. Do you know that the Bosnian Serbs did away with all ideological insignia on their caps?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make, to the best of my recollection in my evidence here, any reference to badges on uniforms. When I did refer to the dress of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Red stars, that's what you said, red stars. I think that's in your statement. But, all right, let's move on. You did not know that the conflict in Bijeljina lasted for two days, on the 1st and 2nd of April. That is on 3983. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you did not know that this conflict was initiated by the Muslim extremists; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a tense here. You're saying I did not know. I'm saying I do not know, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't know that the Serbs were also victims in Bijeljina, that there had been some Serbs that had been killed too; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the conflict -- or, rather, the essence of your understanding of the conflict was the fact that Serbs would not accept the independence of Bosnia. On page 3986, you say that the Serbs accepted the independence of Bosnia on condition that the Lisbon Agreement be honoured; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The witness didn't say that. He said, in fact, when he was asked the question: "Did you know that we made a concession and that we recognised that there was -- that Bosnia was an independent state, and that that -- that was, in fact, the very essence of the Lisbon Agreement?" The witness answered: "No, I didn't know that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Be precise in citing his evidence, Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question was not interpreted properly. The interpretation was not proper. Now we see that. That will be corrected in the final transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 3986, you did not know where the position of Mount Zuc was, and there was fighting around that mountain, and the Muslims took that mountain and they were in a position to fire at all of Sarajevo and Vogosca as well; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Mount Zuc is, Mr. Karadzic, so I guess my answer would have been no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not know that parts of Vogosca that were populated by Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Mr. Karadzic took the witness to the page 3986 and then said, You didn't say something, and then proceeded to misinterpret what was actually said, but then doesn't follow up with a question. And all these questions have been asked and answered already by the witness. We've been going on at this for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I took it that he was about to conclude his cross-examination. But you are just wrapping up his answers. What's the point? Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is to see whether something changed, as far as the memory of the general is concerned. He didn't know a great many things that he had to know, in view of the position he had held, or, rather, he misrepresented things. He ascribed certain things to the Serbs that had been done by the Muslims. I think that's important, and I hope that I will be able to wrap up within the time that you gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, General, on 3988, you did not know that the Serbs controlled Muslim parts of Vogosca; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you now whether you knew that at Ilidza or in Hadzici, the Serbs did not control Muslim parts. In Pale, they did not control Muslim areas. You haven't stated that yet. I'm asking you now: Do you know that the Serbs did not control --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic put to the general, right, on page 3988: "You did not know that the Serbs controlled Muslim parts of Vogosca; right?" That wasn't what was put. The question was: "Did you know that a part of Vogosca is inhabited by Muslims, and that that's a part that Serbs never controlled and that included Kobilja Glava, the area from which they attacked Vogosca?" And the answer was: "No."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He paraphrased in a certain way and the general was able to answer. Let's move on. But I raised it, Mr. Karadzic. I don't see the point of you repeating or wrapping up the previous answers given by the general.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Excellency. Now I'm going to ask my associate to count how many important facts there were that a military adviser has to know, and the general would have to know that. If he did not know that, he could not be a good adviser or a good associate to the mediators in our peace conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's a statement and an assertion. It's not evidence and it's not a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be a good subject for your submission later on, not subject for the cross-examination of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court -- actually, I give up. I'm giving up on almost -- well, actually, it's almost 100 key facts that the general does not know and he had to know about that in view of his important position. Could we have 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No statement. General Wilson, do you have any comment on this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say, Your Honour, that a military adviser doesn't have to know all the facts, but he has to know where to go and find them. And if there was a requirement for specific information or a report, then it was my job to consult with UNPROFOR, for them to look at the records, provide me with advice, and then to pass it to the co-chairman, and I did this on a regular basis. I did not have a detailed knowledge of every event on every day of the conflict in the two years I was there, and I'll openly admit that, Mr. Karadzic, but I knew where to find out if the UN, in fact, knew. And there was a great deal -- there were many unknowns and many grey issues, if you wish, during the conflict. It was impossible to attribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Have your concerns been resolved, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, let's conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 10603, that's the 65 ter number I'd like to have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, General: Did you regularly send reports to Canberra every week?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a requirement from my national authorities, so, yes, in broad terms during 1992, but not during 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the others; did they also send reports to their own governments?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What others are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the other UN representatives from different nationalities. It was a multinational group, so did your colleagues send reports to their governments?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't ask them. It was none of my business. I was required to report on a weekly basis on, essentially, concerning my personal security. Australia had very limited strategic interest in this conflict, and I was only reluctantly released to the United Nations for it. The minister of defence would have been quite happy for me to return to my former duties rather than continue to participate in the event, so my weekly reports were to allow them to assess the security situation and my personal safety. If it was unacceptable, I would have been withdrawn. That was the purpose of them, not to report the operational activities of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this one looks pretty operative to me. Let us look at paragraph 1, for instance. This is what you say: "The past week has been marked by heavy fighting in Sarajevo." And then you say: "Serb forces have continued to shell the city ..." And then further down, you say -- further down. Could we please see the lower part of this page. You say that weapons will be -- actually, you say that observers will focus, and so on and so forth. This is a rather operative report: [In English] "A number of death threats issued against him the last seven to ten days for alleged bias towards the Serbs. It is an interesting city." [Interpretation] That's what you say. So you are aware of these Muslim threats to the UNPROFOR commander, death threats, because he is allegedly biased towards the Serbs. So, General, this is your report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my report. Much of it was actually in the international media at the time. When I'm talking about the detailed deployment of what's happening of UN forces in UNPROFOR, it is because the three majors mentioned, Majors Day, McManus and Tully, are three Australians who are there on temporary deployment from UNSO, the Middle East, so my government is very interested to know how these three Australians are going to be employed in Sarajevo, for the same reason I gave in regard to my own personal security. That's way I have attempted to describe their likely employment. And, yes, there were death threats issued against various UN personnel, including General MacKenzie and myself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document, if it's not an exhibit already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This has been admitted as Exhibit P1034, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have a 65 ter document. 11286 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, General, that the corps commander -- the then corps commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps forbid the use of artillery pieces in the area under the corps and that it could only be used -- exclusively be used if he granted permission?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say he gave permission very often, then, Mr. Karadzic, because the period 14 May to 24 June was a period of intense operational activity, with daily heavy artillery fire into the city of Sarajevo, with very, very few pauses. It was a very liberal interpretation of this directive, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, wouldn't it be necessary to determine who was doing the shooting and then go on from there and say the Serbs were shooting 'round town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I haven't disputed the fact that both sides fired. It's the nature of the fire that's of concern. That the Serbs were disproportionate, inappropriate, widespread in their response, that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if you look at this document, it was issued on the same day as your report. Now, General, if you do not know where the Serb forces were and where the Muslim forces were, and where the Serb settlements were and the Muslim settlements were, how can you report to your government, telling them that it was the Serbs firing? What about if the Muslims fired from Sirokaca, Hum, Zuc, Debelo Brdo and so on, who was the culprit then, who was to blame then? Do you agree that you should have known all this, that you should have known who did the firing? The interpretation is not correct again.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I answered yesterday that it was my assessment that because of the weight of fire that was coming in, that it was attributed to the Serbs; that the Presidency forces did not have the quantity of weapons to produce the amount of fire that was coming -- or that was occurring within the city. That's why it's attributed to the Serbs, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, you said several times that the Serbs were disproportionate, inappropriate, and widespread in their responses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for clarity, what do you mean by being widespread in their response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, technically when artillery fires, it fires in a unit called a battery of six artillery pieces, and it has an area on the ground where it lands, if it's employed correctly, of about 250 by about 250 metres. Usually, it's fired at six rounds at a time so they all land at approximately the same time for maximum effect. That's how good artillery unit fires. Typically, the Serb fire would be spread over -- it might be over a kilometre. The rounds were coming in. There was a mixture of calibres, heavy and light. It didn't appear to be related to any particular target. There was no concentration of fire around -- you know, they didn't appear to have a specific target in mind. It was just the general area that was being fired upon. The example of the mobile mortar, for example. The mobile mortar fired, and I observed it, two rounds or three rounds of fire, and approximately 200 rounds was fired in response. It was an urban area, full of tall apartment buildings. Many of them were hit and set on fire. The distribution of the fire was, as I say, over quite a large area, entirely disproportionate for two rounds to be responded by 100 or more -- perhaps 200 rounds, and such heavy weight of fire that can cause so much damage and so much collateral damage. That's an example, but it's typical of what happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you have no proof of that. Now, do you know that the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not make speeches, Mr. Karadzic. You just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct when I say that you don't have proof of that? Or if you do, show it. Let's see the proof and evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Mr. Karadzic, I saw this with my own eyes. I'm saying it under oath. I can't be more specific than that. I haven't got a film of it. Otherwise, I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that the Serbs took back positions from which they were pushed away from with artillery fire, they took back those positions with artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has been related to me, but I have no specific example of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have evidence of that here. The Muslim side reported that, We were pushed back, and then with long artillery fire the Serbs pushed us back and returned to the trenches. Is that legitimate, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, it depends very much upon where this happened, Mr. Karadzic, whether this happened on the top of an isolated hill or in the middle of an urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Along the lines, the lines from which we were pushed back. And if they passed by, the Serb settlements were destroyed, just like Pofalici. And since the Serbs did not have enough infantry, they used the artillery to push out the Muslim army from their trenches and then they went back to the trenches. Is that legitimate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I return to my earlier point. It depends where in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender that document, 1126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether you asked any question about this or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did ask a question. I asked whether the general knew that the corps commander had prohibited this and that he was the only person who could issue permission, and the general's answer was that, as far as he was concerned, the general issued -- the commander issued permission too frequently. And in the previous document that was admitted, the general said that the Serb forces continued to shell the city, whereas it is my case and I claim that that was just said lightly and that all shells falling from the hills down onto the town was said to be Serb. And the general agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D335, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D1160 displayed next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is one of your documents, General. 1D1860 is the correct number. And if you look at it, you can see how you understood at the time who wanted to achieve what in Sarajevo. And if we look at paragraph 3, one sentence there, and then we'll go on to the next page, it says: [In English] "A BH Army offensive in Sarajevo would appear to remain on hold." [Interpretation] And we're talking about the 22nd of January, 1993. And you know that an offensive was underway launched by the Muslim forces in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you accept that? Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I co-authored this with Brigadier Messervy Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we turn to page 2, please, and I'd ask you to read out paragraph 6. It's a short one.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "No major developments should be expected in the Sarajevo area. Without unacceptable casualties, the capture of the city is an unobtainable objective for the Serbs. The BSA will remain in a defensive posture and rely on superiority in indirect firing weapons to deflect any BH Army offensive."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, General, that at the time you knew that the Serb artillery was used to stop a Muslim offensive; right? You realised that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's not in dispute, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now pan down the page to paragraph 9. I'll read out one sentence: [In English] "BH Army forces will, as a priority, continue to apply pressure to disrupt Bosnian Serb Army lines of communication and strengthen their links to the Srebrenica and Gorazde pockets in eastern Bosnia..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read out, "They would also assist," that sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "They would also assist in ensuring BSA compliance with territorial agreements and place BiH Army forces in an advantageous position for a resumption of hostilities which they probably regard as inevitable."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If Mr. Karadzic can put a question to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably he may put a question after taking on one more paragraph. Let's wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see there paragraph 11 and the second sentence: [In English] "BiH Army forces may ..." [Interpretation] Can you read it out, please, the sentence beginning: "BiH Army forces may ..."

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "BiH Army forces may be prepared to launch an offensive using their troops, without Croat support, if they believe their position in peace negotiations is so weak they must provoke foreign intervention."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now paragraph 13: "In summary, BiH Army forces military objectives are assessed as:" Can you read out points D and E, please, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Launch an offensive in the Sarajevo area if they consider their bargaining position in negotiations untenable and intervention is the only recourse. "E. Continue to re-arm and build up forces and resources for a resumption of the war when they are in a more advantageous position."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you wrote this. Does this show that you knew the situation and that you knew the Muslim army would launch offensives and that it would persevere in those offensives?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is my assessment of the operational situation in January of 1993 and my personal assessment of how I saw this developing. This was my job, to advise the co-chairman of this, and I did this on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very correct assessment. I have no quibbles about that. And I'd like to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I noticed that you make a lot of psychological characterisations of the actors concerned, and you've said probably for the needs of the Krajisnik trial, the case against Krajisnik, that I said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Karadzic repeat that word? I didn't -- could Mr. Karadzic repeat what he just said, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreters are asking you to repeat what you said. They couldn't follow. Take a look at the -- could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You made quite a lot of psychological and moral characteristics of the actors involved, especially the Serbs. And for the requirements of the Krajisnik trial -- against Krajisnik, that is, you said that I consulted him and that he might have even been more important. Now, do you know that every decision by the president, every decision of mine, must have been taken to the Assembly for the Assembly to vote on it and accept it or not? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall you saying in Geneva, Mr. Karadzic, that you had to take at least important decisions to the Assembly. I find it very hard to believe that every decision of yours would have to be taken to some sort of political assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in one of your reports -- in several of your reports, in fact, you are reporting and saying that I'm fighting at the Assembly in Pale to have the constitutional principles adopted from the Vance-Owen Plan. So your report that Karadzic is having problems and that he's fighting in the Assembly to have such major issues presented at the Assembly, that was your report, that I had difficulties in the Assembly; right? That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what report we're talking about, Mr. Karadzic. That's of a political nature. My interest and my responsibilities were on military matters. I find it hard to believe that I'd be talking about your political responsibilities. But if you remind me of the report, I'd be happy to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I just have 15 minutes left, but on some other occasion we shall be offering that up for admission. Anyway, this is a report dated the 28th of August, 1993, as requested by Brigadier Wilson: [In English] "The following is an update of the B and H Assembly ..." [Interpretation] And then you go on to speak about the Bosnian and the Serb Assembly met in Pale: [In English] "The Serb Assembly met in Pale yesterday for the first of two day-long session. Karadzic is pushing hard to have the Geneva package accepted by the delegates. Many of those delegates, however, are arguing strongly against making the territorial concessions called for." [No interpretation]: [In English] "Karadzic is reported to have lost patience with the hard-line delegates, calling some of them paranoid. He is arguing that gains in international legitimacy present the Serbs control approximately 70 per cent of the B and H area. Under the Geneva Agreement, they would end up with 52."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any 65 ter number or the like?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have 1D1857. Can we see that on e-court? And give me a minute or two more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1857 is the document number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that it hasn't been released yet. Shall we put it on the ELMO, then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, because my time is limited and this is, after all, an important document. It's being up-loaded. It's already been up-loaded, so it's already on e-court, but the announcement has not reached us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't see it in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is at our request. It was updated. A meeting of the two assemblies, the Muslim, Croatian, and Serbian Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you show the bottom part? Can you move it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on e-court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see, General, that you did have the information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example of knowing where to ask information, as a military adviser, Mr. Karadzic. I've gone down to Bosnia-Herzegovina Command and asked them to provide information which I would have passed to the co-chairman. There are many hundreds, if not thousands, of these documents which passed my desk in my 12 months in Geneva. I don't recall this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you see, General, here, that I am fighting to reduce the 70 per cent to 52 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the report says, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you see that I'm not finding it easy to get this through the Assembly. I'm struggling against the hard-liners and people who are losing territory; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the job of a good leader, Mr. Karadzic, to get people to do things that they don't necessarily want to do. It's the responsibility of good leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Lord Owen said that it was unprecedented that an army that was not defeated is asked to leave behind such a large portion of territory under its control?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have that piece of evidence here, and we will be showing it in due course. But I'd like to tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D337, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 107 of your report, you said: [In English] "It was normal in dealing with military commanders at a certain level. They were interested in fighting a war and gaining military advantage, not in withdrawing." [Interpretation] Therefore, you can say that you agree that I asked that from 70 per cent of the territory that we controlled, that we could go back to 52 per cent and conclude a peace agreement, and that the deputies were dissatisfied with that, as were the military structures?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you wrote this. You said that the military factor did not like withdrawing, and here it would have to withdraw from 70 per cent of the territory to 52 per cent of the territory, which means that they would have to give up control of 30 per cent of what they were holding; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that paragraph mentions percentages at all, Mr. Karadzic. I haven't got it in front of me, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if you look at paragraph 106, this is what it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show it through e-court or the general can be provided with the statement. Do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to draw the participants' attention to paragraph 106, which starts: [In English] "As a result of the London Conference in 1992, Karadzic agreed that Serbs' heavy weapons in certain locations in Bosnia would be concentrated." [No interpretation]: [In English] "The Bosnian Serb military were unwilling to effect the political agreement that had been reached by their political leaders in London." [Interpretation] And then 107: [In English] "This was normal when dealing with military commanders at a certain level. They were interested in fighting a war and gaining military advantage, not in withdrawing." [Interpretation] And this, then, is the basis for the assertion made by Lord Owen that it was unprecedented in history to see an undefeated army leaving behind a third of the territory that it was otherwise in control of. And that's your statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic, to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question was: Does the general agree that he did have this knowledge to the effect that we were ready to withdraw from 70 per cent of the territory to 52 per cent of the territory, and that I had to struggle, in a democratic assembly, against the deputies, and that the military structures were against this option too? It's logical, and he says it's logical, himself, it was logical for them to oppose that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't know that; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the detail of that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, this statement and your report testifies to the fact that you did. Thank you. Now, General, you mentioned that we accepted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You made another statement. Would you like to comment on that statement, General Wilson? You have a separate observation, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. In addition, Your Honour, I just want the record to be clear. Back on page 25, lines 25, Mr. Karadzic put: "But in one of you're reports -- in several of your reports, in fact, you're reporting and saying that I'm fighting at the Assembly." When you look at -- it's clear, Your Honours, to see the document that he then showed General Wilson, which has now been marked as D337, is not authored by the witness. It's, in fact, authored -- drafted by David Harland and says "as requested by Brigadier Wilson," but this is David Harland's comments, not the general's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic put such complex questions to me. Sometimes I can find five or six elements. If some of them are inaccurate, then I can only answer no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether you would like to comment upon his statement that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, I'm totally unaware of what percentage of territory was involved, and it changed weekly, daily, during negotiations in Sarajevo, and people went into great detail, sometimes moving a line on a map a kilometre or two. So it depends on what time Mr. Karadzic is talking about. I am aware that Mr. Karadzic did from time to time try and sell a particular agreement to the Serb political assembly in Banja Luka. Whether he was successful or not, I don't know the reason for that because I was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, of course, you would stand by what you stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did -- I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But on page 30 of this report of yours -- or, rather, on page 4 of the transcript, you confirmed the need to obtain urgent information on specific operational activities as they affected ongoing negotiations. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which -- what document we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about that list of the roles of a military adviser. Point C was this, to do what I've just read out, and you confirmed that earlier on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of my jobs to obtain information for the co-chairman about ongoing operational matters, yes, and military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you asked Harland to inform you about what was going on in the Serb Assembly, and Harland informed you that Karadzic was facing problems to get approval for the Serb side to reduce its territory from 70 per cent to 52 per cent; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to show me the document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The document that was in e-court a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but I can't recall seeing in that document the two percentages. I didn't take it -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have it in e-court? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this: "Karadzic is pushing ..." You don't have to read it out loud. Just look at the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in accordance with paragraph C, were you not informed? And when you were not informed, you asked Harland to inform you about what the Serb position essentially was in relation to the territory that was under its control; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have another 15 minutes or so, Excellency? It would be better if I could have an entire session. There are many documents that are important, like this one, and that we will not have time to deal with otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You wasted so long a time putting unnecessary questions this morning. I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much do you have, Ms. Sutherland, for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At this stage, Your Honour, I think 10 minutes, but I want to consult with Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour, and you will have 15 minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, remember that yesterday we looked at some documents where I referred to the reasons why the Serbs cannot be left without any artillery around Sarajevo, and that my position was that if the artillery were to withdraw, the Muslim army would try to break through and kill all our civilians. Remember, we showed that yesterday? 1D1870. In the meantime, could I have that on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with your position on this matter, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to see what the Command of the 1st Corps is ordering towards the end of your stay there, on the 8th of December, 1993. We also have a translation of this document. I would like to draw your attention to number -- actually, before number 2, this section: "The battalion that mostly consists of local people and refugees from the Zenica region, and it does not have full establishment composition, has suffered considerable difficulties -- significance losses in the fighting to date." So see this -- we are the enemy, they are writing this about us, and they are saying that we are under-manned. I would like to draw your attention to number 2 as well. You see what the objective is of the 1st Corps against the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. The Sarajevo Romanija Corps is going to defend itself from attacks in the area of responsibility of the 5th Motorised Brigade and the 102nd Motorised Brigade. Their objective is to take the Nedzarici area and create favourable conditions for moving further towards Ilidza. So they want to take all these Serb areas; isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written in this document, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was at the time while you were there. Were you aware of that? That was at the time when you were involved with the conference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right at the very end of my time then, Mr. Karadzic. I think I actually, on the 8th of December, handed over my duties to General Pellnas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that it was on the 13th or 12th of December, but all right. Let us see, please, what the commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina decided. As we know, the corps was deployed in Sarajevo. I would like to draw your attention to what he decided, especially the sentence that reads: "Creating panic among Chetniks and civilians, launch an attack along certain lines." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we move on to the next page? I think that's the way it is in English too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: See, they even turned schools into military facilities. Did you know that, General, that schools and kindergartens in Sarajevo had been transformed into military facilities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think those schools had had children in them for almost two years by that stage. They were formerly a school, would perhaps be more accurate. There were no longer children going to school in Sarajevo in late 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree, all of those schools had no children there. But when they say that Serbs responded with fire at the school, then nobody says that these are schools where there are no children and that were actually turned into military facilities; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention and the attention -- actually, I'd like to draw the attention of all the participants to the entire document. But could you please look at paragraph 6 now, "Firing Support." We can also have the Serbian version for the benefit of the interpreters. That would be the next page. Just look at what the 1st Corps has at its disposal, the fire support that the units will have, those that intend to break into Serb neighbourhoods. Do you see that, General? There's a reference to the brigades, the 5th and 102nd Motorised Brigades, and so on, the 101st and so on. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It talks about units, but it doesn't describe their size. I mean, you can have a battalion which might be fully equipped and manned, and it could be quite strong or it could be quite hollow with very few forces. It's a name, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As adviser to the mediators, did you know what the actual force of the 1st Corps was? You say 15.000. I say 80.000. Did you know that their three divisions had between 60.000 and 80.000 men? That's the 1st Corps of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends, Mr. Karadzic. When we're talking about -- I gave an estimate of 15.000 at the beginning of the conflict in April/May. I assume you're now talking about the end of 1993. It's quite conceivable that that 15.000 had grown significantly through the opportunity to train and, no doubt, the acquisition of additional weapons. It could well be in that order, but I can't confirm your number. I do not know the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, the participants should see what they have here. See, General, from Mount Igman -- you see that from the previous paragraph and this paragraph. From Mount Igman, artillery will fire at Sarajevo; right? It was the previous paragraph, but it's also in the next paragraph too, number 15, "Command and Communications." The Communications Centre from Mount Igman and so on and so forth, 15.3. Do you see that, sir? The police is also involved in the operations carried out by the 1st Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what's written in the document, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. During the negotiations, you had some information, and on the basis of that information you advised the co-chairman as to what the objectives should be and what the balance of forces was; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave them my assessment of what it was, and I was able to repeat information provided to me by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted? Can we have 1D1866?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Following your guide-lines, Your Honour, I don't think that this document should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we are concerned about your use of time. The general did not know anything about this document, except for some schools which he knew incidentally, so we will not admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you see this document?
